html: Making friends with our afflictions

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: I don't want to do this. All right — then Shantideva goes off on an entire discussion on what mental afflictions do to us. What do they do to us? Which is literally every negative thing that's running through your mind.

Let's go to slide 17, Brian. The problem is that, in some sadistic way, we make friends with our greatest enemies. We make friends with our negativities, our mental afflictions — what we call them in old Buddhism. And in some way we're attached to them. Somehow we like them. Somehow we think they're part of us. We don't want them, but we do want them. When you really look at it, if you didn't want it, you would do all the things to stop it. But somehow we entertain these negativities, and we give them homes. And there's a million reasons why we do that. You can look at your own particular flavor for that. We all have it. But we make friends with it, when we shouldn't be making friends with them.

And how do we then navigate all that? And how does he define it? That's the interesting thing — how does he define it? Next slide, Brian. A mental affliction, a negativity, is anything that ruins your peace of mind. And that's a very subtle thing to say. In this picture, this guy's trying to meditate and his kids are not allowing him. That's what's going on in your head every single time you're trying to do some kind of high spiritual practice, and you're trying to do something good because you're actually convinced of it. You're here, you're in class. We're all in class. You spend hours listening to these things — you wouldn't spend hours listening to me blah-blah about this if you didn't already think it was useful for you. But then when you actually turn to practice — that's what we were talking about in the last class, or earlier: the space between the thinking and the action. The gap. The listening and the doing. It's the same thing. You're already convinced; you don't have to be convinced anymore. But the moment you try to practice and you're like, I'm going to do this — it's like this all the time. The noise in our experience is just tremendously overwhelming.

Everyone knows, the first time you try to meditate — and the first complaint you have to your teacher is, I've been meditating and my mind is just getting worse and worse. I'm not getting better, I'm getting worse. And then the teacher starts laughing: you're not getting worse. You're just listening for the first time. You're just listening to what was already there and you just didn't notice it.

It's like one of my good friends — our karmic partner — we've been focusing on issues of health. Duh, Tim — have a karmic partner and maybe things get better. And they have been, because I have a karmic partner now. We were talking about eating, and we recognized how important diet is to our health. And we tried the experiment: we took sugar out of our diet — all processed sugar, very little fruit, no candies, no sodas, no ice creams, no sugar in coffees. It was complete. Take it all out. And then you notice the things that have a lot of carbohydrates in them that you didn't realize had carbohydrates. You're just constantly eating these things that aren't good for your body. But once you take it out and go through this process, then when you put it back in, you feel what it actually does to you.

I remember we had a meeting with my karmic partner and they said, yeah, I was driving late, and I was super tired, so I stopped at the gas station and I got a bottle of Coca-Cola to stay awake. I was like, oh, how'd that go? And they said, oh my God, I felt terrible. The caffeine helped a little bit, but the sugar — and the sugar in Coca-Cola is not sugar, it's poison sugar. If you really look at it, it's no good for you. Sorry — I know you like to drink it, I used to like to drink it too. You're young; when your body revolts, you'll stop drinking it. But don't get to a point where your body revolts — just stop now. But basically, what it did to their body — they could feel the sugar rise, they felt terrible, they went to bed, and then three hours after going to bed they had a crash. They woke up in the middle of the night, they felt terrible, they were incredibly hungry, they raided the refrigerator. And then they were like, oh my God, I didn't realize what this was doing to my body.

Like this week — I haven't been drinking coffee for eight months, and I was like, let me just try this out, what does the caffeine do to my body? Oh my gosh. I can feel the intensity. But I didn't feel it before. Was it doing it before? Yes — you just didn't notice.

And that's what happens with our spiritual practice. We start to do it, and then all of a sudden we're like, oh my God, it's a jungle in here. It's a zoo in here. My life is a zoo. Just chaotic animals running everywhere. And that's what happens. Then you start recognizing that, wow, there's a lot of work to do — and it becomes a lot. And then what happens to a lot of people is the application becomes so much that they can't hold on to it, or they don't want to continue, or they're not seeing the changes they want to see yet. Just imagine if you looked at your zoo and none of the animals had cages for eons. You're trying to put them in cages, you're trying to feed them in the right way, you're trying to create order. It's going to take some time. It's going to be mayhem for quite a while. You don't need the motivation to be in class. You need the motivation to do it. That's the hard part.
The six root afflictions

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So what are the six afflictions that get in our way? Slide 19. Liking things ignorantly. Basically, this means that you want things but you don't know how to get them, and so you just take them. Like this donut — just take it, and didn't know how you got the donut in the first place.

Next slide. The opposite: disliking things and ignorantly trying to push away things you don't like, in the wrong way, with misunderstanding. How do you make a problem go away? You just yell at somebody. Was that really the cause of that problem? Did the yelling stop the problem? If the yelling stopped the problem, then every time you yelled at someone it would stop all the problems. How do you get rid of things you don't like? Again, it's the whole thing about understanding the real cause versus the apparent cause. But this is what's happening in our mind all the time. The zoo in our mind — it's not even a zoo, it's like Jurassic Park Island when they turn off all the gates, and all the animals just break out, and everyone's running around trying not to get eaten by the velociraptors. Do you know how to say velociraptor in your language? It's kind of like a Tyrannosaurus Rex, I don't know. They're all just running around, and you're trying to capture a wild dinosaur that just wants to eat you. It's going to be a little while — because everything you want and everything you don't want, we've been trying to get and get rid of in a wrong way. And then you're trying to clear up your mind in the wrong way too. Sorry to drop that bomb. You're trying to capture that velociraptor in your mind, and you're not even using seeds. You think you're using seeds, but you're not. Where does good meditation come from? Use the V Houses app. No — it comes from taking care of other people's minds first.

All right, third main mental affliction, negativity, pride. This one's amazing. We all have this, and it takes many forms. The way I like to think of it for myself is that I am the hero of my own story. I'm the center of my universe — which is kind of true in some ways. But it takes on different flavors for different people. Like that feeling that somehow I'm right and you're wrong. Or I'm better than you in some way. It's subtle, but this little comparison — because you want to feel important. Your mind is designed to make you feel important. Parentheses — I didn't say you weren't important. I didn't say that. But this kind of pride is a protection mechanism. And in some way you feel important in such a way that you're willing to do it to hurt other people — to judge other people, to think bad things about them, to get things ignorantly, et cetera, et cetera. So Shantideva is like, look at yourself, look at this. I don't know what dinosaur would be a pride dinosaur.

All right, next one is just general ignorance. Kids are like this — they don't want to listen to their dad or their parents. La la la la la, I can't hear you. That's literally us all the time. La la la la la. Not coming this way — it's coming this way. It's just the way it goes.

All right, next one is doubt. Te-tsom [THE TSOM]. Doubt about wisdom. Doubt in yourself. The doubt that you can do it. The lack of belief in yourself. This is like the opposite of pride. Pride is like, I'm awesome and you're not. Doubt is like, I'm actually not awesome, and I'm never going to do anything with it — which is in some ways a kind of pride too. But a lot of this is about doubt that the truth can help you.

And then the next one, Brian, are just wrong views in general. And there's five or six of them, and it would take a whole class to go through all of those. But it's all the ways that we misunderstand karma and emptiness — karma and its consequences, excuse me. Misunderstanding the parts of you. Extreme views. Thinking that wrong views are the correct views. Your pride is also mixed up with wrong views — they're all mixed up, it's all jumbled together. And then thinking that doing things to hurt yourself is the best spiritual practice — like self-deprecation, hurting yourself to get ahead spiritually.
Is hatred of afflictions itself an affliction?

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So there's this fun thing. Next slide. Gyaltsab Je says: well, someone comes along and says, isn't love and dedication for the path, and then hatred of your mental afflictions, also a mental affliction? Is it also not ignorant — not wanting your mental afflictions, and then wanting enlightenment in the wrong way, because we're not arhats? Isn't that an affliction itself? Pretty smart debater. It's like, oh — you're just using mental afflictions to point out that... you're using mental afflictions to actually try to get out of samsara? Are you kidding me? You're just playing with your mind, planting more seeds for it. Your hatred for your mental afflictions is not a mental affliction. Come on. I understand the question.

And so what he says is — how does he say it? Let me make sure I got it correct. It's sort of like what I was saying earlier about the Matrix. You have to use elements of it to turn itself over itself — use the elements that are present to kind of break it. And he says, hatred for your mental afflictions is not something you want to eliminate; you want to continue to battle those. Love for the path is something that you want to battle for — they are part of the path. Being unhappy with your ignorance is probably a good thing. You may not be there yet — which is kind of what the question earlier was: I'm not there yet, I feel hopeless. That's okay. We're not there yet. But that's part of the path to get there. So the path itself uses certain kinds of energies that are in deceptive reality to then unwind the whole thing — just like the Matrix. Now use it against itself. And then eventually those things disappear. Because as those negativities disappear, then your hatred for the thing that's not there disappears, because it's not there anymore to hate. That makes sense. Eventually you have to let that go — but you let it go because you've already come to some kind of stopping of them, so then there's no need to have it anymore. You let it go when there's no need.
Cutting the root: the misperception

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: And then Shantideva says: why? How is the continued appearance of some kind of negativity dependent upon a misperception? And why is it important that we know that the continued existence of your negativity depends upon a misperception? Your anger, as it goes on, depends upon a misperception. Your pride depends upon that. But why is it important to know that?

What's on the screen right now? Something from Mars? No. This is the Je Tsongkapa mantra. And I want to focus on the first part here: mik-me tse-we [DMIGS MED BRTZE BA'I]. Which is love that doesn't see. It's love that doesn't see anything.

So why is it important that we know that the continued existence of a mental affliction is dependent upon a misperception? Because once you eradicate the misperception, you eradicate the negativity. Eyes that don't see anything — what does that mean? It's not like they're looking out into the void and not seeing, seeing black, black, black. That's not what that means. An eye that doesn't see anything, love that doesn't see anything — understands where it's coming from in the first place: that it wasn't there to begin with, on its own, from its own side, independent of how you treated others in the past. Because the eyes that see that absence — that absence of its own existence, independent...

What Shantideva is saying is, look, you can spend all your time focusing on pride, or your anger, or your jealousy, or all the other 20 — there's 20 other secondary mental afflictions. You can do all the seeds for that. You can spend all your time being like, I feel hopeless, or I feel this or that, or I don't know why I have to see this. You can do all that — and that's part of the process. But once you eradicate the misperception, all of that other stuff just vanishes completely. The root of it just vanishes. If you take away the root, the rest of the tree can't stand. If all of our negativities are based upon a misperception, focus at the root. Don't worry about, should I plant seeds for money or a partner and all of that other stuff — I didn't say don't do that. I didn't say don't help other people. But can you infuse all of that with — and dedicate those seeds to — removing your misunderstandings? Everything you do serving other people can be dedicated to eradicating that misperception, pulling that misperception out, pulling that root out. And then you have the eye of wisdom, and all that other stuff just evaporates. Anytime you get close to those negativities, you just go, no, no, no, no. And then it just loses its power and grip over you.
